title: BASS (PSI-26)
text: Burned fabric (cotton-fiberglass SIBAL), acrylic (PMMA), Nomex, Ultem and candles in a small ISS glovebox flow duct, in air flowing with or against the flame, and tested a CO₂-like extinguishing agent. Key result: 74 of 110 runs kept burning, 10 went out and 8 never lit; fabric spread up to 5.1 mm/s in the 7.6 cm duct. Tested: O₂ 16%–23%, pressure 0.97–1.01 atm, fuels: Cotton-fiberglass, Japan wax, Nomex III, Nomex blend, PMMA, Ultem, paraffin wax.

title: BASS (PSI-26): hardware, samples, instruments and variables
text: Hardware: Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) with the fan-driven flow duct built for SPICE. Samples or burners: candle, fabric sheet, sphere, thick slab (+1 more); width 1 cm to 2 cm. Measured with: flame spread, extinction, suppression. Instruments: digital still camera through the top window (about 1 frame/s), video camera through the front window (30 frames/s), hot-wire anemometer for flow speed, wide-angle radiometer inside the duct (Ferkul et al. 2013). Changed between tests: fuel or material: Cotton-fiberglass, Japan wax, Nomex III, Nomex blend (+3 more); sample or burner shape: candle, fabric sheet, sphere, thick slab (+1 more); O₂: 16% to 23% (39 values); pressure: 0.97 atm to 1.01 atm (24 values); air speed: 0 cm/s to 30 cm/s (22 values); flow direction: concurrent, opposed, stagnation, wake ignition; sample width: 1 cm to 2 cm (2 values). Held the same: nothing recorded as constant.

title: BASS-II (PSI-25)
text: Follow-on to BASS: acrylic slabs, rods and spheres, fabric and candles burned at different air speeds and oxygen levels to find when a flame starves or blows off. Key result: 129 tests mapped a ‘Goldilocks’ window: 12 flame-outs, from flames starving at low air speed and blowing off at high speed. Tested: O₂ 14%–22%, pressure not recorded per test, fuels: Cotton-fiberglass, Japan wax, Nomex, PMMA.

title: BASS-II (PSI-25): hardware, samples, instruments and variables
text: Hardware: Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) with the fan-driven flow duct built for SPICE. Samples or burners: candle, fabric sheet, rod, slab (+4 more); thickness 0.10 mm to 5.00 mm; diameter 6.3 mm to 40.0 mm; width 1 cm to 2 cm. Measured with: flame appearance, growth, spread rate, extinction; O2/CO/CO2 readings. Instruments: video with flow speed, fan and radiometer overlay; Nikon D300s still camera; O₂ sensor; CDM CO₂ sensor and CSA-CP CO analyser (BASS-II data FAQ and science requirements document). Changed between tests: fuel or material: Cotton-fiberglass, Japan wax, Nomex, PMMA; sample or burner shape: candle, fabric sheet, rod, slab (+4 more); O₂: 14% to 22% (50 values); air speed: 0 cm/s to 28 cm/s (16 values); flow direction: concurrent, opposed; thickness: 0.10 mm to 5.00 mm (9 values); diameter: 6.3 mm to 40.0 mm (4 values); sample width: 1 cm to 2 cm (2 values). Held the same: nothing recorded as constant.

title: Saffire-I (PSI-98)
text: The first large spacecraft fire: a 94 × 40 cm cotton-fiberglass sheet burned inside an empty Cygnus cargo ship after it left the ISS, to see how fast a big fire grows. Key result: The large fabric sheet burned in microgravity, spreading up to 1.8 mm/s with the flow, at measured cabin pressure. Tested: O₂ 22%, pressure 1.01 atm, fuels: Cotton-fiberglass.

title: Saffire-I (PSI-98): hardware, samples, instruments and variables
text: Hardware: Saffire flight hardware inside an uncrewed Cygnus cargo vehicle. Samples or burners: flat sheet; thickness 0.37 mm; width 41 cm; length 94 cm. Measured with: large-scale flame spread rate, mass consumption, heat release. Instruments: two cameras viewing the front of the sample; thermocouples at the duct inlet and outlet, embedded in the sample and in the plume; radiometers viewing the front and back of the sample; solid-state CO₂, O₂ and pressure sensors in the avionics bay; an anemometer on each side of the sample; a smoke wire at the sample's leading edge for flow uniformity (SAFFIRE-II readme, Table 3: Saffire I, II and III diagnostics). Changed between tests: O₂: 21.5% to 21.6% (2 values); flow direction: concurrent, opposed. Held the same: fuel or material: Cotton-fiberglass; sample or burner shape: flat sheet; pressure: 1.01 atm; air speed: 20 cm/s; thickness: 0.37 mm; sample width: 41 cm; igniter power: 182 W.

title: Saffire-II (PSI-99)
text: Nine 5 × 29 cm samples (silicone, cotton-fiberglass fabric, acrylic, acrylic joined to Nomex), the same size as NASA's 1 g screening test (NASA-STD-6001 Test 1), burned on Cygnus to compare microgravity flammability limits with that test. Key result: Silicone burned on Earth but did not spread in microgravity (4 of 4 samples); Nomex did not burn; fabric and acrylic did. Tested: O₂ 22%, pressure 1.02 atm, fuels: Cotton-fiberglass, Nomex, PMMA, Silicone.

title: Saffire-II (PSI-99): hardware, samples, instruments and variables
text: Hardware: Saffire flight hardware inside an uncrewed Cygnus cargo vehicle. Samples or burners: flat sheet; thickness 0.27 mm to 10.00 mm; width 5 cm; length 5 cm to 29 cm. Measured with: low-g flammability limits vs NASA 1 g test. Instruments: two cameras viewing the front of the sample; thermocouples at the duct inlet and outlet, embedded in the sample and in the plume; radiometers viewing the front and back of the sample; solid-state CO₂, O₂ and pressure sensors in the avionics bay; an anemometer on each side of the sample; a smoke wire at the sample's leading edge for flow uniformity (SAFFIRE-II readme, Table 3: Saffire I, II and III diagnostics). Changed between tests: fuel or material: Cotton-fiberglass, Nomex, PMMA, Silicone; O₂: 21.5% to 22.1% (4 values); air speed: 20 cm/s to 25 cm/s (2 values); flow direction: concurrent, opposed; thickness: 0.27 mm to 10.00 mm (6 values); igniter power: 80 W to 97 W (2 values). Held the same: sample or burner shape: flat sheet; pressure: 1.02 atm; sample width: 5 cm.

title: Saffire-III (PSI-100)
text: A second large cotton-fiberglass sheet burned on Cygnus, with flow in both directions. Key result: The large fabric sheet burned in microgravity, spreading up to 2.3 mm/s with the flow, at measured cabin pressure. Tested: O₂ 21%, pressure 0.98 atm, fuels: Cotton-fiberglass.

title: Saffire-III (PSI-100): hardware, samples, instruments and variables
text: Hardware: Saffire flight hardware inside an uncrewed Cygnus cargo vehicle. Samples or burners: flat sheet; thickness 0.37 mm; width 41 cm; length 94 cm. Measured with: flame spread at different flow conditions. Instruments: two cameras viewing the front of the sample; thermocouples at the duct inlet and outlet, embedded in the sample and in the plume; radiometers viewing the front and back of the sample; solid-state CO₂, O₂ and pressure sensors in the avionics bay; an anemometer on each side of the sample; a smoke wire at the sample's leading edge for flow uniformity (SAFFIRE-II readme, Table 3: Saffire I, II and III diagnostics). Changed between tests: flow direction: concurrent, opposed. Held the same: fuel or material: Cotton-fiberglass; sample or burner shape: flat sheet; O₂: 21%; pressure: 0.98 atm; air speed: 25 cm/s; thickness: 0.37 mm; sample width: 41 cm; igniter power: 182 W.

title: ACME BRE (PSI-20)
text: A porous gas burner that imitates burning solids, run in still air at the spacecraft atmospheres NASA has considered (14.7 psia/21 %, 10.2 psia/26.5 %, 8.2 psia/34 %). Key result: Emulated solids kept burning in still air at raised oxygen, while flames at 21 % O₂ went out on their own (investigation page). Daily summaries only, no per-flame results. Tested: O₂ 21%–40%, pressure not recorded per test, fuels: C2H4, C2H4 50% in N2, CH4.

title: ACME BRE (PSI-20): hardware, samples, instruments and variables
text: Hardware: ACME modular hardware in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR). Samples or burners: porous burner 25 mm, porous burner 50 mm; size 25.0 mm to 50.0 mm. Measured with: heat flux, flame height/radius, radiative fraction, extinction. Instruments: heat-flux sensor and burner surface temperature (investigation page). Changed between tests: fuel or material: C2H4, C2H4 50% in N2, CH4; sample or burner shape: porous burner 25 mm, porous burner 50 mm; O₂: 21% to 40% (5 values). Held the same: air speed: 0 cm/s; flow direction: none. Although it burned gas, BRE is a materials-flammability study: the burner imitates a burning solid, in still air, as a function of material properties.

title: FLEX (PSI-69)
text: Free-floating fuel droplets (heptane, methanol and others) burned on the ISS to map when liquid-fuel flames go out and how well CO₂ and helium suppress them. Key result: 274 droplet tests; 17 ran at 29-34 % O₂ and about 0.7 atm, the closest any investigation came to the habitat air; CO₂ and helium were tested only up to 25% O₂. Tested: O₂ 12%–34%, pressure 0.69–3.05 atm, fuels: methanol, n-heptane.

title: FLEX (PSI-69): hardware, samples, instruments and variables
text: Hardware: Multi-user Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA) in the CIR. Samples or burners: droplet; initial droplet diameter 1.1 mm to 4.7 mm. Measured with: LOI, droplet burning rate, extinction diameter, cool flames. Instruments: droplet imaging for burning rate and extinction size, heat radiation, soot and temperature (investigation page goals). Changed between tests: fuel or material: methanol, n-heptane; O₂: 12% to 34% (15 values); pressure: 0.69 atm to 3.05 atm (182 values); droplet size: 1.1 mm to 4.7 mm (163 values); CO₂ added: 0% to 70% (14 values); helium added: 0% to 45% (10 values). Held the same: sample or burner shape: droplet; air speed: 0 cm/s; flow direction: none.

title: FLEX-2 (PSI-68)
text: Follow-on to FLEX with fuel mixtures closer to real fuels, droplet arrays and soot, over 0.5-3 atm and up to 40 % O₂. PSI lists its condition ranges, not per-test results. Key result: Catalogued from its PSI record; per-test results not loaded. Tested: O₂ 10%–40% (PSI range), pressure 0.50–3.00 atm (PSI range), fuels: real-combustor-like fuels and mixtures.

title: FLEX-2 (PSI-68): hardware, samples, instruments and variables
text: Hardware: Multi-user Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA) in the CIR. Samples or burners: droplet / droplet arrays (catalog, from the NASA page or listing). Measured with: burning rate, sooting, extinction, multi-droplet. Instruments: colour camera video; chamber pressure and temperature (investigation page). Changed between tests: per-test data not loaded. Held the same: per-test data not loaded.

title: CFI (PSI-39)
text: Droplets of n-dodecane, n-dodecane/iso-dodecane mixtures and farnesane, suspended between needles or on silicon-carbide fibres and lit by a retracting hot wire, to study cool flames (the dim low-temperature flame that can outlast the visible one): how pressure, helium dilution and droplet size change burning and extinction, and how soot forms. Key result: 79 test conditions loaded (conditions only). Tested: O₂ 17%–21%, pressure 0.50–5.00 atm, fuels: n-dodecane, n-dodecane/iso-dodecane 0.60/0.40, n-dodecane/iso-dodecane 0.75/0.25.

title: CFI (PSI-39): hardware, samples, instruments and variables
text: Hardware: Multi-user Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA) in the CIR. Samples or burners: droplet, droplet (fiber-supported), droplet (free (needle-deployed)); droplets suspended between hypodermic needles or tethered on silicon-carbide fibres; hot-wire igniter retracted after ignition (investigation page). Measured with: cool-flame burning and extinction. Instruments: black-and-white camera for droplet size; UV camera for OH* emission and flame size; narrow-band and wide-band radiometers for flame radiation; high-resolution cameras for monitoring (investigation page). Changed between tests: fuel or material: n-dodecane, n-dodecane/iso-dodecane 0.60/0.40, n-dodecane/iso-dodecane 0.75/0.25; sample or burner shape: droplet, droplet (fiber-supported), droplet (free (needle-deployed)); O₂: 17% to 21% (2 values); pressure: 0.50 atm to 5.00 atm (7 values); helium added: 0% to 59% (3 values). Held the same: air speed: 0 cm/s; flow direction: none. The NASA page lists farnesane and pressures from 0.25 atm; the PSI table we loaded holds n-dodecane and two n-dodecane/iso-dodecane mixtures at 0.5-5 atm (the page itself gives both 0.25-5 and 0.25-0.5 atm). Sponsored by the ISS National Laboratory and NSF.

title: Cool-flame counterflow (FLEX) (PSI-142)
text: Cool-flame transitions near radiation and stretch extinction in counterflow flames. Key result: Catalogued from its PSI record; per-test results not loaded. Tested: O₂ not listed, pressure not listed, fuels: n-alkanes (counterflow).

title: Cool-flame counterflow (FLEX) (PSI-142): hardware, samples, instruments and variables
text: Hardware: ground lab + model; builds on data from PSI-69. Samples or burners: counterflow (catalog, from the NASA page or listing). Measured with: cool-flame extinction limits vs O2 (3 numerical models). Instruments: none of its own: a model or analysis investigation that uses data from PSI-69. Changed between tests: per-test data not loaded. Held the same: per-test data not loaded.

title: Cool-flame CFD (FLEX) (PSI-117)
text: Droplet cool-flame measurements and simulations (heptane, decane, dodecane) and how outside disturbances change them. Key result: 72 measurements and simulations of droplet cool flames used in the droplet model. Tested: O₂ 10%–21%, pressure 0.50–5.00 atm, fuels: n-decane, n-dodecane, n-heptane.

title: Cool-flame CFD (FLEX) (PSI-117): hardware, samples, instruments and variables
text: Hardware: model + FLEX data; builds on data from PSI-69; PSI-142. Samples or burners: fiber-supported droplet; size 0.5 mm to 7.0 mm. Measured with: cool-flame dynamics, extinction diameters, burning rate vs pressure. Instruments: none of its own: a model or analysis investigation that uses data from PSI-69; PSI-142. Changed between tests: fuel or material: n-decane, n-dodecane, n-heptane; O₂: 10% to 21% (2 values); pressure: 0.50 atm to 5.00 atm (8 values). Held the same: sample or burner shape: fiber-supported droplet; air speed: 0 cm/s; flow direction: none; ambient temperature: 298 K.

title: SAME (PSI-102)
text: Overheated (not burning) spacecraft materials made smoke in the ISS glovebox, to see how big microgravity smoke particles get and whether smoke detectors notice them. Key result: 20 smoke test conditions, all in cabin air (21 % O₂, 1 atm); results are in raw files not loaded. Tested: O₂ 21%, pressure 1.00 atm, fuels: Dibutyl Phthalate, Kapton, Lampwick, Silicone Rubber, Teflon.

title: SAME (PSI-102): hardware, samples, instruments and variables
text: Hardware: Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) with the SAME smoke hardware. Samples or burners: heated sample (smoke generator). Measured with: smoke particle size distribution, detector response. Instruments: two smoke detectors, video cameras, thermophoretic samplers whose particles were sized by TEM after flight (investigation page). Changed between tests: fuel or material: Dibutyl Phthalate, Kapton, Lampwick, Silicone Rubber (+1 more); air speed: 5 cm/s to 10 cm/s (2 values). Held the same: sample or burner shape: heated sample (smoke generator); O₂: 21%; pressure: 1.00 atm; flow direction: through-flow. One SAME instrument, a modified P-Trak, was used to measure dust in DAFT and DAFT-2.

title: SAME-R (PSI-101)
text: Reflight of SAME with new materials (Pyrell foam), hotter heating and no-flow runs, after SAME's particle samples came back contaminated. Key result: 67 smoke test conditions, all in cabin air (21 % O₂, 1 atm); results are in raw files not loaded. Tested: O₂ 21%, pressure 1.00 atm, fuels: Kapton, Lampwick, Pyrell, Silicone, Teflon.

title: SAME-R (PSI-101): hardware, samples, instruments and variables
text: Hardware: Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) with the SAME smoke hardware. Samples or burners: heated sample (smoke generator). Measured with: smoke particle sizes vs heating, detector performance. Instruments: the SAME instruments plus a new in-house instrument (M-pass); clean TEM grids after SAME's contamination (investigation page). Changed between tests: fuel or material: Kapton, Lampwick, Pyrell, Silicone (+1 more); air speed: 0 cm/s to 8 cm/s (5 values); heating time: 60 s to 120 s (2 values); smoke aging time: 1 s to 720 s (3 values). Held the same: sample or burner shape: heated sample (smoke generator); O₂: 21%; pressure: 1.00 atm; flow direction: through-flow. One SAME instrument, a modified P-Trak, was used to measure dust in DAFT and DAFT-2.

title: SAME smoke model (PSI-115)
text: Modelling and simulation of smoke generation in microgravity using SAME data. Key result: Catalogued from its PSI record; per-test results not loaded. Tested: O₂ not listed, pressure not listed, fuels: dibutyl phthalate (DBP).

title: SAME smoke model (PSI-115): hardware, samples, instruments and variables
text: Hardware: model; builds on data from PSI-102. Samples or burners: pyrolysis smoke (catalog, from the NASA page or listing). Measured with: simulated smoke particle growth, 1 g vs 0 g. Instruments: none of its own: a model or analysis investigation that uses data from PSI-102. Changed between tests: per-test data not loaded. Held the same: per-test data not loaded.

title: SPICE (PSI-107)
text: Gas jet flames (methane, ethylene, propane, propylene and propylene mixtures) from 0.41, 0.76 and 1.6 mm nozzles in co-flowing air: the fuel flow was raised until each flame started releasing soot (its smoke point), to measure how burner size, air speed and fuel change sooting. Key result: 469 fuel-flow settings from 142 flame runs, all in cabin air; smoke points are in raw files not loaded. Tested: O₂ 21%, pressure 1.00 atm, fuels: 50% Propylene, 75% Propylene, Ethylene, Methane, Propane, Propylene.

title: SPICE (PSI-107): hardware, samples, instruments and variables
text: Hardware: Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) with the fan-driven flow duct built for SPICE. Samples or burners: round jet nozzle 0.41 mm, round jet nozzle 0.76 mm, round jet nozzle 1.60 mm; size 0.4 mm to 1.6 mm. Measured with: smoke point, soot formation 0 g vs 1 g. Instruments: still and video cameras; measured flame height (luminous length), radiative heat loss and co-flow air velocity distribution; a flow duct with integrated nozzles and fuel delivery in the glovebox (investigation page). Changed between tests: fuel or material: 50% Propylene, 75% Propylene, Ethylene, Methane (+2 more); sample or burner shape: round jet nozzle 0.41 mm, round jet nozzle 0.76 mm, round jet nozzle 1.60 mm; air speed: 0 cm/s to 85 cm/s (61 values); fuel flow: 0.00 mg/s to 4.40 mg/s (275 values). Held the same: O₂: 21%; pressure: 1.00 atm; flow direction: co-flow. NASA's page gives co-flow speeds of 5.4-65 cm/s and 526 flames; the PSI table we loaded has 469 settings, 26 of them listed outside that speed range (0-85 cm/s). Values are shown as tabulated.

title: SPICE soot analysis (PSI-60)
text: Computational and experimental analysis of the SPICE soot data sets. Key result: Catalogued from its PSI record; per-test results not loaded. Tested: O₂ not listed, pressure not listed, fuels: SPICE fuels.

title: SPICE soot analysis (PSI-60): hardware, samples, instruments and variables
text: Hardware: model + image analysis; builds on data from PSI-107. Samples or burners: co-flow jet (catalog, from the NASA page or listing). Measured with: soot temperature/volume fraction (color-ratio pyrometry). Instruments: none of its own: a model or analysis investigation that uses data from PSI-107. Changed between tests: per-test data not loaded. Held the same: per-test data not loaded.

title: SLICE (PSI-106)
text: How gas jet flames anchor and lift off in co-flowing air, for methane, ethylene and nitrogen-diluted mixtures (12 test days). Key result: Catalogued from its PSI record; per-test results not loaded. Tested: O₂ 21%–21% (PSI range), pressure 1.00–1.00 atm (PSI range), fuels: CH4 (20-100% in N2), C2H4 (20%/100%), C2H6, C3H8.

title: SLICE (PSI-106): hardware, samples, instruments and variables
text: Hardware: Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) with the fan-driven flow duct built for SPICE. Samples or burners: jet burner tubes in coflow (catalog, from the NASA page or listing). Measured with: flame structure, liftoff, stability. Instruments: over 4,000 high-resolution flame images over 13 test days (investigation page). Changed between tests: per-test data not loaded. Held the same: per-test data not loaded.

title: ACME CLD Flame (PSI-21)
text: Methane and ethylene flames burning in a gentle coflow of air, from very dilute to heavily sooting, to measure flame shape, lift-off, temperature, extinction limits and soot as velocity and fuel dilution change, and to test computer models of soot. Key result: Catalogued from its PSI record; per-test results not loaded. Tested: O₂ not listed, pressure not listed, fuels: methane and ethylene, diluted to sooting.

title: ACME CLD Flame (PSI-21): hardware, samples, instruments and variables
text: Hardware: ACME modular hardware in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR). Samples or burners: coflow burner: a fuel jet surrounded by a slow coflow of air (investigation page). Measured with: flame shape, lift-off height, temperature, extinction limits, soot luminosity, soot temperature and volume fraction. Instruments: OH* and CH* chemiluminescence imaging for lift-off and flame shape; soot luminosity and laser extinction for soot temperature and volume fraction; thin-filament pyrometry for gas temperature (investigation page). Changed between tests: fuel (methane, ethylene), fuel dilution (dilute to heavily sooting) and flow velocity (investigation page). Held the same: coflow burner in the ACME hardware (investigation page). E-FIELD Flames (PSI-22) used this same coflow burner for its coflow tests (PSI-22 page).

title: ACME CFI-G (PSI-159)
text: Spherical gas flames (ethane, propane, butane) in a closed, still chamber from 18 to 40 % O₂ and 0.5 to 3 atm: does a flame ignite, and does it go out by itself? Key result: In still air, all 41 flames at ≤25 % O₂ went out by themselves (median 8 s); at 33-40 % O₂ the median was 50 s and 30 of 91 were still burning when the fuel was cut. Tested: O₂ 18%–40%, pressure 0.50–3.00 atm, fuels: 30% ethane, 30% n-butane, 30% propane, 50% n-butane, ethane, propane.

title: ACME CFI-G (PSI-159): hardware, samples, instruments and variables
text: Hardware: ACME modular hardware in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR). Samples or burners: spherical porous burner (normal flame). Measured with: cool diffusion flame conditions (normal/inverse). Instruments: cameras, radiometers, photomultiplier tubes (PMTs) and thermocouples (investigation page). Changed between tests: fuel or material: 30% ethane, 30% n-butane, 30% propane, 50% n-butane (+2 more); O₂: 18% to 40% (121 values); pressure: 0.50 atm to 3.00 atm (5 values); fuel dilution: 0% to 100% (14 values); fuel flow: 0.00 mg/s to 3.21 mg/s (25 values). Held the same: sample or burner shape: spherical porous burner (normal flame); air speed: 0 cm/s; flow direction: none. CFI-G ran the highest oxygen levels in microgravity: in inverse flames an oxygen-nitrogen mix of up to 85 % O₂ flowed from the burner into a chamber of nitrogen and fuel. Our table holds only the normal flames (fuel from the burner, 18-40 % O₂ around it), which is the cabin-like case.

title: ACME Flame Design (PSI-10)
text: Spherical ethylene and methane flames, normal (fuel from the burner) and inverse (oxidizer from the burner), in drop towers and on the ISS: when soot starts to form and when the flame goes out, as flow rate, mixture fraction (Zst), N₂ or CO₂ dilution and pressure change. Key result: Catalogued from its PSI record; per-test results not loaded. Tested: O₂ not listed, pressure not listed, fuels: ethylene and methane, with N2 or CO2 inert.

title: ACME Flame Design (PSI-10): hardware, samples, instruments and variables
text: Hardware: ACME modular hardware in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR). Samples or burners: spherical burner for normal and inverse spherical flames; coflow flames as well (investigation page). Measured with: soot-inception and extinction limits, flame temperature, size, colour, soot volume fraction. Instruments: cameras, radiometers, photomultiplier tubes and thermocouples (investigation page). Changed between tests: fuel (C₂H₄, CH₄), flow rate, stoichiometric mixture fraction Zst, inert (N₂ or CO₂) amount, pressure, and flame direction (normal or inverse) (investigation page). Held the same: spherical burner in the ACME hardware (investigation page). Flame Design also ran inverse spherical flames, where the oxidizer flows from the burner, like the CFI-G inverse flames. Its hypothesis: microgravity spherical flames go out once their peak temperature drops below 1130 K. Tests ran in drop towers as well as on the ISS.

title: ACME s-Flame (PSI-23)
text: Hydrogen, methane and ethylene, diluted with nitrogen, helium or CO₂, issued from a spherical porous burner into an oxidizing environment: the structure of soot-free and sooty spherical flames, their extinction limits and pulsating instabilities, compared with detailed simulations. Key result: Catalogued from its PSI record; per-test results not loaded. Tested: O₂ not listed, pressure not listed, fuels: hydrogen, methane and ethylene, diluted with N2, He or CO2.

title: ACME s-Flame (PSI-23): hardware, samples, instruments and variables
text: Hardware: ACME modular hardware in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR). Samples or burners: spherical porous burner giving a nominally spherical, one-dimensional flame (investigation page). Measured with: flame structure (temperature, species), growth, extinction limits, pulsating instabilities, soot suppression. Instruments: spectrally resolved flame imaging, flame and burner temperatures, radiative flux, and operating conditions (reactant flow rates, ambient temperature, pressure, acceleration levels), all synchronized (investigation page). Changed between tests: fuel/diluent mixture (H₂/CH₄/diluent for soot-free flames, C₂H₄/diluent for sooty ones), diluent (N₂, He, CO₂) and flow rate (investigation page). Held the same: spherical porous burner in the ACME hardware (investigation page).

title: ACME E-FIELD Flames (PSI-22)
text: Methane and ethylene flames (diluted with nitrogen) in an electric field of up to 10 kV between the burner and a mesh above it, with and without a coflow of air: how the field drives ions in the flame, changes its stability and soot, and how fast it responds. Key result: Catalogued from its PSI record; per-test results not loaded. Tested: O₂ not listed, pressure not listed, fuels: methane and ethylene, diluted with N2.

title: ACME E-FIELD Flames (PSI-22): hardware, samples, instruments and variables
text: Hardware: ACME modular hardware in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR). Samples or burners: gas-jet burner, and the coflow burner shared with ACME CLD Flame; copper mesh electrode above the burner (investigation page). Measured with: ion current vs voltage, flame response time, flame shape and luminosity, soot volume fraction, chemiluminescence, radiant emission. Instruments: high-resolution cameras for flame shape, luminosity and soot; spectral imaging with filters for chemiluminescence and soot volume fraction; thermopile detectors for radiant emission; recorded voltage-current curves (investigation page). Changed between tests: fuel (methane, ethylene), nitrogen dilution (stable to near-extinction flames), fuel flow rate, coflow velocity (with and without coflow), field strength (up to 10 kV) and polarity (investigation page). Held the same: the ACME hardware in the CIR; mesh electrode above the burner (investigation page). The challenge brief notes that this experiment mimicked partial gravity: the field acts on the ions that flames make naturally (chemi-ionization) and drives ion-driven convection, a stand-in for buoyancy. Its coflow tests used the same burner as ACME CLD Flame (PSI-21). Per-test data are not in PSI's tables we loaded.

title: BASS flame-spread model (PSI-62)
text: A computer model of concurrent flame spread compared with BASS flame measurements. Key result: Catalogued from its PSI record; per-test results not loaded. Tested: O₂ not listed, pressure not listed, fuels: BASS samples.

title: BASS flame-spread model (PSI-62): hardware, samples, instruments and variables
text: Hardware: model + BASS images; builds on data from PSI-25; PSI-26. Samples or burners: flat (catalog, from the NASA page or listing). Measured with: concurrent flame spread model validation. Instruments: none of its own: a model or analysis investigation that uses data from PSI-25; PSI-26. Changed between tests: per-test data not loaded. Held the same: per-test data not loaded.

title: Saffire IV-VI (external) (EXT-SAFFIRE-456)
text: Saffire IV to VI on Cygnus: fabric, cotton, acrylic and Nomex burned in reduced-pressure, oxygen-rich air (54-71 kPa, 26-31 % O₂), with cabin CO₂ and CO measured. Published in NASA reports, not in PSI. Key result: The only solid-fuel burns near habitat air: fabric, cotton and acrylic burned at 26-31 % O₂ and 0.53-0.70 atm, Nomex did not ignite; burning acrylic raised cabin CO₂ by 8,117-8,539 ppm. Tested: O₂ 22%–31%, pressure 0.53–0.99 atm, fuels: Cotton jersey, Cotton-fiberglass, Nomex fabric, PMMA.

title: Saffire IV-VI (external) (EXT-SAFFIRE-456): hardware, samples, instruments and variables
text: Hardware: Saffire flight hardware inside an uncrewed Cygnus cargo vehicle. Samples or burners: fabric sheet, thick slab (1-sided burning), thick slab (2-sided burning); thickness 0.37 mm to 10.00 mm; width 41 cm; length 7 cm to 50 cm. Measured with: far-field CO₂ and CO measurements used for the cabin-air results (Urban et al. 2024, Table 2). Changed between tests: fuel or material: Cotton jersey, Cotton-fiberglass, Nomex fabric, PMMA; sample or burner shape: fabric sheet, thick slab (1-sided burning), thick slab (2-sided burning); O₂: 22% to 31% (5 values); pressure: 0.53 atm to 0.99 atm (5 values); thickness: 0.37 mm to 10.00 mm (3 values). Held the same: air speed: 20 cm/s; flow direction: concurrent; sample width: 41 cm.

title: What makes a still-air flame last longer
text: +1 % oxygen: burn time ×1.17; +0.1 atm pressure: burn time ×0.97; double the fuel flow: burn time ×0.65; +10 % fuel in the fuel stream: burn time ×1.04; propane instead of ethane: burn time ×0.60; n-butane instead of ethane: burn time ×0.65. Oxygen dominates: each extra 1 % O₂ makes a flame last about 17 % longer.

title: What decides whether a solid keeps burning
text: Air speed matters most: flames starve at very low airflow and blow off at high airflow. Then material. Inputs ranked: Air speed, Material, Oxygen, Shape, Pressure, Flow direction. Each +1 % O₂ multiplies the odds of sustained burning by 1.54.

title: Moon and Mars gravity
text: All tests here ran in microgravity (ISS, Cygnus) or, for comparison, on Earth. No PSI investigation has burned anything at lunar (0.16 g) or Martian (0.38 g) gravity, so for Moon and Mars surface habitats these results are the nearest evidence, not a measurement.

title: Partial gravity: No partial-gravity fire data in PSI yet
text: No PSI combustion investigation has burned anything at lunar (0.16 g) or Martian (0.38 g) gravity. NASA expects such data from the Lunar-g Combustion Investigation (LUCI) and Flammability of Materials on the Moon (FM2).

title: Partial gravity: LUCI: simulated lunar gravity on a sounding rocket
text: LUCI burned a cotton-fiberglass (SIBAL) fabric and a 4 mm acrylic (PMMA) rod in air at normal pressure while the Blue Origin New Shepard capsule spun at about 11 rpm to imitate lunar gravity: the first extended (over 25 s) burns in simulated lunar gravity. The acrylic flame tip spread at about 1.5 mm/s. Results are in NASA presentations, not in PSI.

title: Partial gravity: FM2: the first fire experiment on the Moon
text: FM2 will burn four samples, one at a time, in atmospheres planned for lunar habitats, with cameras and temperature, O₂ and CO₂ sensors. Drop-tower centrifuge tests behind it found that some materials burn at lower oxygen levels in lunar gravity than on Earth: less heat loss than at 1 g, yet enough buoyant flow to feed the flame.
source: NASA FM2 page; Zayac et al., NTRS 20240015307 (2024), https://www.nasa.gov/flammability-of-materials-on-the-moon-fm2/

title: Partial gravity: Mimicked partial gravity: ACME E-FIELD Flames (PSI-22)
text: A field of up to 10 kV between the burner and a mesh above it pushes on the ions a flame makes (chemi-ionization), driving ion-driven convection that stands in for buoyancy; microgravity lets this be studied without real buoyancy. That makes E-FIELD Flames the closest PSI comes to partial gravity. Its per-test data are not in the tables loaded here.
source: PSI-22 investigation page; challenge brief, https://doi.org/10.60555/se5a-8c73

title: Partial gravity: Bounding with 0 g and 1 g, and its limit
text: Microgravity and Earth results can bracket intermediate gravity: where a material behaves the same at both, that is the best available guess for the Moon. But the FM2 work shows the bracket is not always safe, since some materials are most flammable at lunar gravity. Materials whose 0 g and 1 g results disagree should be tested first.
source: Challenge brief; Zayac et al., NTRS 20240015307, https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20240015307

title: Saffire materials at 0 g and 1 g: bounding partial gravity
text: Cotton-fiberglass: microgravity burned in 6 of 6; spread 1.0-2.6 mm/s; Earth burned in 4 of 4; spread kept accelerating; bounds agree: burns at any gravity. Nomex: microgravity burned in 0 of 1; Earth no result recorded; not enough results. PMMA: microgravity burned in 3 of 3; Earth burned in 2 of 2; spread kept accelerating; bounds agree: burns at any gravity. Silicone: microgravity burned in 0 of 4; Earth burned in 3 of 3; spread 0.6-1.2 mm/s; spread kept accelerating; bounds disagree: partial gravity unknown, test it first.

title: Shared hardware: ACME modular hardware in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR)
text: The six ACME experiments all burned gaseous fuels with the same modular ACME hardware in the CIR, so their conditions and diagnostics are directly comparable. Investigations: PSI-20, PSI-159, PSI-21, PSI-10, PSI-23, PSI-22
source: NASA Space Apps 2026 challenge brief; Ferkul et al. 2013 (BASS duct); PSI investigation pages and the SAFFIRE-II readme (PSI-99); catalog/investigations.csv

source: NASA Space Apps 2026 challenge brief; Ferkul et al. 2013 (BASS duct); PSI investigation pages and the SAFFIRE-II readme (PSI-99); catalog/investigations.csv

title: Shared hardware: Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) with the fan-driven flow duct built for SPICE
text: BASS, BASS-II, SPICE and SLICE shared one modular fan-driven duct in the glovebox, so solid and gas flames were burned in the same controlled air flow. The duct is 76 mm × 76 mm in cross-section (Ferkul et al. 2013). Investigations: PSI-26, PSI-25, PSI-107, PSI-106
source: NASA Space Apps 2026 challenge brief; Ferkul et al. 2013 (BASS duct); PSI investigation pages and the SAFFIRE-II readme (PSI-99); catalog/investigations.csv

title: Shared hardware: Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) with the SAME smoke hardware
text: SAME and SAME-R heated materials until they smoked and passed the smoke to detectors. One of their smoke instruments, a modified P-Trak, was first checked in the Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Tests (DAFT and DAFT-2), which measured dust instead of smoke (challenge brief; NASA Glenn Combustion Science page). Investigations: PSI-102, PSI-101
source: NASA Space Apps 2026 challenge brief; Ferkul et al. 2013 (BASS duct); PSI investigation pages and the SAFFIRE-II readme (PSI-99); catalog/investigations.csv

title: Shared hardware: Saffire flight hardware inside an uncrewed Cygnus cargo vehicle
text: A sample card sits in the middle of a large flow duct; fans at the top draw air through it past flow straighteners. Burned inside Cygnus after it left the ISS, so a spacecraft-sized fire could be studied without risk to a crew (PSI-99 page). Investigations: PSI-98, PSI-99, PSI-100, EXT-SAFFIRE-456
source: NASA Space Apps 2026 challenge brief; Ferkul et al. 2013 (BASS duct); PSI investigation pages and the SAFFIRE-II readme (PSI-99); catalog/investigations.csv

title: Fire-safety equipment: Smoke and fire detectors
text: 555 smoke and soot tests (SAME, SAME-R, SPICE), all at 21% O₂ and 1 atm. SAME-R's page notes microgravity smoke particles may be larger and fool detectors; an earlier flight showed the Shuttle detector missing smoke it caught in 1 g. Next generation: Calibrate detectors on smoke made in habitat air; the size shift means 1 g calibration is not enough.

title: Fire-safety equipment: Extinguishers and suppressants
text: CO₂ and helium suppression of droplet flames: 173 FLEX tests, at up to 25% O₂. The ISS replaced its CO₂ extinguishers with fine-water-mist ones, because CO₂ was unsafe with the crew's emergency breathing equipment. Next generation: Test suppressant amounts at 30-34 % O₂ before relying on them in a habitat.

title: Fire-safety equipment: Ventilation shutdown procedures
text: In still air, all 41 CFI-G flames at ≤25 % O₂ went out by themselves; at 33-40 % O₂, 30 of 91 were still burning when the fuel was cut. BRE saw emulated solids keep burning without air flow at raised O₂. Next generation: In an oxygen-rich habitat, pair fan shutdown with active extinguishing.

title: Fire-safety equipment: Material selection and screening
text: BASS-II mapped flames starving at low air speed and blowing off at high speed (12 flame-outs). Saffire-II silicone burned in its 1 g comparison burns but not in microgravity; at lunar gravity some materials burn at lower oxygen than at 1 g (FM2 work). Next generation: Screen habitat materials at habitat O₂, pressure, air speed and gravity, not only NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 in Earth air.

title: Fire-safety equipment: Air quality: scrubbers and crew masks
text: Burning acrylic (PMMA) on Cygnus raised cabin CO₂ by 8,117-8,539 ppm, several times more than fabric. In BASS-II's ISS burns, thick PMMA slabs raised CO by a median 335 ppm per burn, fabric by about 20 ppm. Next generation: Size CO₂ and CO removal and masks for plastic fires.
source: Saffire VI (Urban et al. 2024, Table 2); BASS-II test matrix (PSI-25)

title: Fire-safety equipment: Enclosure and layout
text: The same fabric in nearly the same air spread 1.8 mm/s in a 51 cm duct and 5.1 mm/s in a 7.6 cm duct. Next generation: Treat racks, ducts and stowage gaps as higher-risk zones for detection and suppression.
source: Saffire I-IV, BASS; Olson et al., Table 1

title: Which materials make the most carbon monoxide when they burn (BASS-II)
text: CO rise per ISS burn, median: PMMA slab (1-5 mm) 335 ppm (19 tests); Clear PMMA rod 135 ppm (25 tests); PMMA spherical section 80 ppm (2 tests); Black PMMA rod 56 ppm (24 tests); Japan wax candle 34 ppm (1 tests); SIBAL cotton-fiberglass fabric 20 ppm (25 tests); Thin PMMA film (0.1-0.4 mm) 16 ppm (20 tests); Nomex fabric -10 ppm (2 tests). Measured inside the closed Microgravity Science Glovebox, not a cabin: initial and final O₂, CO₂ and CO for each BASS-II test (PSI-25 test matrix). Gases built up from one test to the next, so each test is scored by its own rise (final minus initial). Burn times and sample sizes differ. The O₂ sensor was corrected with a constant offset from the ISS reading; CO readings marked over range (about 1,000 ppm and above) or '>500' are counted but not averaged (BASS-II data FAQ).

title: Fire safety on Earth: Fine-water-mist extinguishers
text: NASA funded the development of a fine-water-mist portable extinguisher for the ISS; nine replaced the carbon-dioxide extinguishers that did not suit the crew's emergency breathing equipment, the last arriving in 2016. Its zero-leak valve now stops leaks in industries on Earth, and the same valve is used in the extinguisher being developed for Orion.

title: Fire safety on Earth: Smoke detection
text: Spacecraft smoke detectors were first designed from Earth tests. A NASA flight experiment found the Shuttle detector could be blind to smoke it caught in 1 g, showing detector design cannot rely on 1 g experience; SAME and SAME-R then measured microgravity smoke particles to design better detectors, and NASA work compares spacecraft detector sensitivity with residential UL 217/268 standards.

title: Fire safety on Earth: Firefighter air tanks
text: NASA's composite overwrapped pressure vessels, built for spacecraft, made firefighters' breathing tanks lighter: one 26-pound composite cylinder held as much air as a 41-pound steel one. Composite cylinders are now commonly used by firefighters.
source: NASA Spinoff, 'Public Safety' (spinoff.nasa.gov/node/11031); NASA tech-transfer article, https://spinoff.nasa.gov/node/11031

title: Fire safety on Earth: Firefighter protective clothing
text: After Apollo 1, NASA contracted for fire-resistant PBI textiles for spacesuits and vehicles (1967). Through NASA's Project FIRES they reached US fire services, and PBI fabric is now used in firefighter turnout gear.

title: Scope: rockets and propellants
text: Out of scope: fires involving rockets and propellants. Gas speeds in rocket engines are so high that their combustion is effectively independent of gravity, and PSI holds little research on them (challenge brief).

title: Spacesuit, Earth and Moon base atmospheres: why habitats use oxygen-rich air
text: Earth, sea level (and the ISS): 21 % O₂ at 14.7 psi. Normal air. Spacesuit: 100 % O₂ at 4.3 psi. Low pressure keeps the suit flexible; astronauts pre-breathe pure O₂ first to purge nitrogen and avoid the bends. Moon base and pressurized rovers (expected): 30 % or more O₂ at 10.2 psi or less. Between suit and Earth air, to shorten pre-breathing before moonwalks. Over 40 % more oxygen fraction than Earth air (30/21 = 1.43), so materials burn more readily.
source: NASA Space Apps 2026 challenge brief (Flame in Freefall); NASA atmospheres in ACME BRE (PSI-20)

title: Suppression at habitat oxygen
text: CO₂ and helium suppressant tests on droplet flames only go up to 25 % O₂: putting out a fire with these agents at 30-34 % O₂ is untested.

title: Next experiment: Flammability and spread of cabin solids (PMMA, cotton, Nomex, foams) at 28-32 % O2, 0.6-0.8 atm, 0-20 cm/s air
text: No PSI solid-fuel burn above 22 % O2; only 5 burns lie near the habitat atmosphere (Saffire V-VI, NASA literature). Models cannot score cotton, Nomex or silicone.

title: Next experiment: Smoke-detector response to smoke made at 30 % O2 and 0.69 atm
text: SAME, SAME-R and SPICE: 86 smoke tests and 469 soot-point settings, all at 21 % O2 and 1 atm.

title: Next experiment: Still-air self-extinction of gas and emulated-solid flames at 24-33 % O2
text: ACME CFI-G has no tests between 24 % and 33 % O2, exactly where the habitat sits; burn time rises about 4.6x from Earth air to habitat air.

title: Next experiment: Release per-test FLEX-2 results (multicomponent droplets, 0.5-3 atm, up to 40 % O2)
text: FLEX-2 covers the habitat atmosphere on paper, but only its condition ranges are published in PSI.

title: Next experiment: Repeat key fabric and plastic burns at lunar (0.16 g) and Martian (0.38 g) gravity
text: No PSI combustion investigation has burned anything at partial gravity, so Moon and Mars surface decisions rest on microgravity and Earth tests alone.

title: PSI-10 investigation page: Approach
text: Perform spherical diffusion flame tests in drop towers and aboard the International Space Station. Consider a broad range of reactant dilutions, flow rates and pressures for normal and inverse convection directions. Observe the flames with a broad suite of cameras, radiometers, photomultiplier tubes, and thermocouples.

title: PSI-10 investigation page: Hypothesis
text: 1. Soot formation requires a region where local C/O ratio and T exceed their critical values, and where strain rate is sufficiently low. 2. Microgravity spherical diffusion flames extinguish when the peak temperature first decreases below 1130 K. 3. Steady-state spherical diffusion flames are possible.

title: PSI-10 investigation page: Research Impacts
text: This project has the potential for improving efficiency and reducing pollutant emissions in terrestrial combustors. For example, it is contributing to novel designs of future coal power plants.

title: PSI-101 investigation page: Objectives
text: Similar to the original SAME investigation, the primary objective of the SAME-R investigation was to quantify the sizes that the liquid smoke particulate achieves in low gravity and to relate the droplet size distribution to the smoke generation and smoke transport conditions in the experiment. One of the problems encountered during the SAME investigation was that after the thermal precipitators were returned to the ground, it was found that all the TEM grids were severely contaminated with some unidentified foreign particles, making these grids unusable although some of them showed shapes of certain types of smoke particles. Based on that experience the SAME-R investigation employed several modification covering new materials, extended operating conditions, and diagnostic equipments.

title: PSI-101 investigation page: Approach
text: SAME-R utilized the SAME hardware used on-orbit. Based on the experience gained from SAME, SAME-R included the following modifications: 1) a new test material, Pyrell®, an intumescent fire-retardant foam by Foamex, was introduced to replace DBP samples, 2) test conditions were broadened including higher heating temperatures and no-flow during sample heating time, and 3) a new instrument, M-pass, developed in-house GRC, was used to replace one of the two Commercial Diagnostic Enclosures that includes a DustTrak and an ionization detector used in SAME. SAME-R flight tests were conducted from July 16, to September 9, 2010, successfully completing 66 test points. After SAME-R flight tests, three major post–flight ground tests were performed to improve data reduction process and to validate the lognormal distribution assumption, the key to the moment method employed by SAME and SAME-R.

The formation of the larger particles is favored by the expected higher vapor concentration and smoke residence times near the source due to the reduced velocities and mixing at μg conditions. title: PSI-101 investigation page: Research Impacts
text: Along with the results from the original SAME investigation, the results from SAME-R can lead to technology for an advanced fire detector for future spacecraft that will be used for long duration missions. SAME will provide quantitative data on the sensitivity of these detectors to reduced gravity smokes that will allow evaluation of the adequacy of these existing technologies using relevant data. The current Fire Prevention, Detection, and Suppression (FPDS) program plan allows for the re-evaluation of future sensor technology, to allow new technology and capability to be utilized. The results from SAME are needed to provide the reduced gravity baseline data against which future detection technology developments can be evaluated. The smoke detectors developed from the results of SAME can also be useful in other extreme environments on Earth, such as submarines or underwater laboratories

text: One of the major goals of this investigation was to quantify the sizes that the liquid smoke particulate achieves in low gravity and to relate the droplet size distribution to the smoke generation and smoke transport conditions in the experiment. A numerical code was to be developed to predict the smoke droplet growth as a function of the fuel pyrolysis rate, the thermodynamic properties of the pyrolysis vapor, and the flow environment.

title: PSI-107 investigation page: Objectives
text: The objective of SPICE is to better understand the complex process of combustion by observing flames in a microgravity environment aboard the International Space Station (ISS) and analogous ground experiments. Specific objectives were: (1) Identify the laminar smoke-point properties of non-buoyant jet diffusion flames under various co-flow conditions in microgravity. (2) Determine the effects of burner diameter and co-flow velocity on the luminous flame lengths and smoke points. (3) Quantify the sooting propensity of different fuels, such as ethylene, propane, and propylene mixtures. (4) Validate the correlation between luminous flame shape and residence time under microgravity conditions. (5) Investigate the impact of air and fuel flow rate variations on smoke point phenomena in space.

title: PSI-107 investigation page: Approach
text: The experimental setup in the microgravity science glovebox consisted of an apparatus with a flow duct with integrated nozzles, cameras, and fuel delivery systems. Fuels tested included methane, ethylene, propane, propylene, and propylene mixtures. Each flame was ignited in a controlled co-flow air environment, with burner diameters of 0.41 mm, 0.76 mm, and 1.6 mm and co-flow velocities ranging from 5.4 cm/s to 65 cm/s. Fuel flow rates were adjusted to identify the smoke point, marked by the flame's transition to emitting soot. Data such as flame lengths were recorded using still and video cameras. Measurements included flame height, radiative heat losses, and co-flow air velocity distributions. In total 526 flames were studied.

title: PSI-107 investigation page: Hypothesis
text: The research hypothesizes that by minimizing gravity-driven transport phenomena scientists can study the laminar smoke-point properties of non-buoyant jet diffusion flames. Flame properties are expected to differ significantly from those observed under normal gravity.

title: PSI-107 investigation page: Research Impacts
text: (1) Will improve our understanding of soot formation mechanisms and help design safer spacecraft environments. (2) Will contribute to refining our computational models for predicting flame behaviors under non-buoyant conditions. (3) Will enhance our knowledge of soot generation (4) Could possibly provide insights to better fuel formulations and combustion processes.

title: PSI-20 investigation page: Objectives
text: The BRE flight program seeks to establish the burning conditions in a quiescent microgravity ambient in terms of material properties. The specific flight objectives are as follows. 1. Observe burning behavior in long-duration microgravity for CH4/N2 and C2H4/N2mixtures on porous circular burners of 25 and 50 mm diameter. Consider O2/N2 ambients with various pressures and ambient O2 concentrations and pressures. NASA - considered atmosphere for human space missions will be examined: 14.7 psia, 21 % oxygen: 10.2 psia, 26.5 %; and 8.2 psia, 34 % oxygen. Emphasize fuel conditions that can be related to a diverse range of condensed fuels. 2. Consider the conditions of Objective 1 for ambients of O2/CO2 (desired). 3. Consider the conditions of Objectives 1 – 2 for extinction limits.

title: PSI-20 investigation page: Approach
text: To accomplish the above objectives, flight experiments are proposed. Additionally, preliminary flight tests will be performed to verify the experiment operations and for comparison with ground-based tests. For each test, conditions will be established for the chamber contents, namely choice of diluent, oxygen concentration, and pressure. Fuel flow will commence followed by ignition. The flames will initially be observed without varying the fuel flow rate. Because burner surface temperature and heat flux will vary, this will allow a broad range of conditions to be observed during a single test. As the surface temperature of the burner increases, and the flame remains steady, a continuous set of data is produced for the flammability map. title: PSI-20 investigation page: Hypothesis
text: The BRE investigation hypothesizes that there can exist a regime of quasi-steady burning in microgravity as a function of materials properties. Steady burning may never be achieved, and only slowly changing unsteady flames are possible. The proposed tests aboard the ISS aims to query this hypothesis by establishing a range of quasi-steady burning conditions for condensed fuels in the microgravity environment. It is hypothesized that BRE can determine a range of burning conditions in microgravity as a function of heat of gasification, reradiation heat flux, applied radiant heat flux, heat of combustion and smoke point. This could enable the Cone Calorimeter (NASA Test 2) test as a basis for establishing flammability maps for real materials. title: PSI-20 investigation page: Research Impacts
text: BRE yielded important data relevant to spacecraft fire safety. Quasi-steady burning corresponding to various condensed-phase materials (such as PMMA and Nylon) was observed in microgravity despite the absence of air flow, where the cessation of ventilation is an established step in putting out spacecraft fires. The ongoing combustion without air flow was notably seen in elevated-oxygen atmospheres which are being considered for use in future spacecraft, whereas such flames in a normal atmosphere of 21% oxygen self-extinguished in a short time. While BRE’s results are still preliminary, they suggest that NASA may want to increase use of its alternative flammability Test 2, with the cone calorimeter, where that test can measure material properties corresponding to the microgravity flames observed with the BRE burner.

title: PSI-21 investigation page: Objectives
text: In order to provide the experimental data needed to allow rigorous testing of computational models at the extremes of the fuel dilution spectrum, we have the following objectives: A) Characterize the behavior of weak coflow diffusion flames of methane and ethylene, as a function of velocity and fuel dilution, through measurement of flame shape, lift-off heights, temperatures and extinction limits. B) Characterize the sooting tendencies of diffusion flames with long residence times, as a function of velocity and fuel dilution, through measurement of flame shape, gas temperatures in the soot-free portion of the flame, soot luminosity, soot temperatures, and soot volume fractions.

title: PSI-21 investigation page: Approach
text: ACME CLD Flame project goals include the generation of improved computational models with improved soot sub-models that are effective for both dilute flames and sooting flames that vary from low to high soot loading levels. The enhanced time and spatial scales in a microgravity environment will be important for achieving both goals. Experimentally, we plan to study methane and ethylene diffusion flames over a wide range of test conditions. For the more dilute flames, measurements will be made of flame chemiluminesence of OH* and CH* to observe variations in lift-off height and flame shape as extinction limits are approached. The sooting tendencies of the more fuel-rich flames will be investigated using soot luminosity and laser extinction measurements to determine soot temperatures and soot volume fractions. title: PSI-21 investigation page: Research Impacts
text: Diffusion flames are the flame type of most practical combustion devices. The ability to predict the coupled effects of complex transport phenomena with detailed chemical kinetics in such systems is critical in the modeling of turbulent reacting flows and in understanding the processes by which soot formation and radiative transfer take place. title: PSI-22 investigation page: Approach
text: The E-FIELD flames experiment investigates how electric fields influence the behavior of laminar diffusion flames in microgravity. This unique environment is ideal for isolating electric field effects from buoyancy forces. The experiment is conducted with gas-fueled flames, both with and without a coflow of air. An electric field is generated by creating a high voltage (up to 10 kV) differential between the burner and a flat circular mesh suspended above (i.e., downstream of) the burner. title: PSI-22 investigation page: Hypothesis
text: The application of electric fields in microgravity environments will significantly influence laminar diffusion flames by enabling precise manipulation of flame stability, soot behavior, and combustion dynamics through ion-driven convection and chemi-ionization processes.

title: PSI-22 investigation page: Research Impacts
text: The E-FIELD Flames research is not being conducted to serve any space applications, but it is possible that its findings could aid the development of future space-based combustion devices (e.g., for solid waste processing). The use of electric fields to control flames can reduce the production of harmful pollutants in practical terrestrial combustion. The combustion of fossil fuel is the primary human source of greenhouse gas and acid rain and furthermore creates soot, which can be beneficial but is also a health hazard. Combustion using electrical fields may also allow for more efficient combustion, reducing fuel consumption in addition to unwanted emissions.

title: PSI-23 investigation page: Research Impacts
text: The impact of this work consists of both practical and fundamental aspects. Practically, with diffusion flame burning as the basis in many combustion engines and devices, understanding the underlying dynamics and chemistry of diffusion flames is important in improving performance in terms of power, efficiency, pollutant emissions, and reliability. Fundamentally, the unique buoyancy-free environment offered by microgravity affords simple aerodynamic flow fields to acquire diffusion flame data of high fidelity, with the prospect of understanding unit thermochemical processes as well as quantifying the associated physico-chemical parameters.

title: PSI-69 investigation page: Hypothesis
text: The primary hypothesis of the FLEX mission is that microgravity conditions fundamentally alter the combustion and extinction characteristics of liquid fuel droplets due to changes in species and energy transport dynamics, radiative heat loss, and chemical kinetics. Specifically, the hypothesis posits that the lack of buoyant convection in microgravity will lead to significant differences in the flammability limits and suppression efficacy of various fire suppressant agents compared to normal gravity conditions. This hypothesis underpins the design of the FLEX experiments, which aim to map flammability boundaries, quantify suppressant efficacy, and develop predictive models to improve fire safety in space environments.

title: PSI-69 investigation page: Research Impacts
text: The research impacts and Earth benefits of the FLEX mission are significant and multifaceted. By enhancing our understanding of microgravity combustion, the mission directly contributes to improved fire safety protocols for future space missions, ensuring the safety of crew members in environments where traditional fire suppression methods may be ineffective. On Earth, the insights gained from these experiments have the potential to advance fire safety in confined and reduced-gravity environments, such as submarines or high-altitude aircraft. title: PSI-98 investigation page: Hypothesis
text: This investigation hypothesizes that due to large differences between fire behavior in normal and reduced gravity, the use of terrestrial fires and fire standards to design spacecraft fire safety systems presents an inherent risk to the vehicle because of the significant level of uncertainty. While this approach has been successful thus far, the uncertainty and risk will increase as exploration missions venture further from earth with considerably longer transit times for a safe return. There is a significant lack of microgravity data available for spacecraft designers on which to base their fire safety designs and procedures. To address this knowledge gap, this investigation proposed to conduct large-scale fire safety experiments in an expendable spacecraft without risk to a crew.

title: PSI-98 investigation page: Research Impacts
text: The Saffire-I experiment provides a new way to study a realistic fire on an exploration vehicle, which has not been possible in the past because the risks are too high. Instruments on an unmanned cargo vessel measure oxygen, carbon dioxide, heat, pressure and flame growth, and two video cameras provide views of the flame. Results determine microgravity flammability limits for several spacecraft materials, help to validate NASA’s material selection criteria, and how microgravity and limited oxygen affect flame size. The investigation is crucial for the safety of current and future space missions. Studying fire in small, sealed environments such as the Cygnus cargo supply vehicle benefits fire safety and prevention efforts on Earth, including inside mines, airplanes, or submarines.
